analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal to gouge prices on gasoline and other fuels during declared energy emergencies.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 41 cosponsors including one Republican, never received a hearing or a vote and died in subcommittee in June 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful, during an energy emergency the President declares, to sell gasoline or other petroleum fuels at unconscionably excessive prices. It would give the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general power to fine violators — up to three times the illegal profits or $3 million — and let the Justice Department pursue criminal penalties of up to $150 million for corporations. Money from fines would go into a fund to help low-income households pay heating and energy bills.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, and farm, commercial, and residential fuel customers, who would gain a federal backstop against price spikes during emergencies like hurricanes or supply disruptions. State attorneys general would gain a new federal law to enforce on behalf of their residents, and low-income households would benefit because all collected fines flow into the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and low-income energy assistance households

how_it_helps.text: During a Presidentially declared energy emergency, it would be unlawful to sell gasoline or other petroleum fuels at a price that is 'unconscionably excessive' or shows the seller is taking unfair advantage of the emergency, protecting motorists at both wholesale and retail levels [S2][S3].

The FTC and state attorneys general could enforce the ban, with civil fines of up to three times the violator's illegal profits or $3 million, and the Justice Department could bring criminal cases carrying fines up to $150 million for corporations and up to 10 years' imprisonment for individuals [S2][S3].

The bill directs the FTC to prioritize enforcement against the largest companies — those with more than $500 million a year in wholesale or retail fuel sales — so the biggest fuel sellers face the most scrutiny [S3].

All fines and penalties collected would go into a Consumer Relief Trust Fund to pay for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, turning enforcement penalties into heating and energy bill help for low-income households [S2][S3].
The bill explicitly does not preempt state law, so states could keep or strengthen their own anti-gouging rules, and states could sue on behalf of their residents in federal court [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies, refiners, wholesalers, and gas stations selling fuel during declared emergencies, which would face civil fines up to three times their excess profits or $3 million and criminal fines up to $150 million. Legitimate sellers could also face litigation costs if the vague 'unconscionably excessive' standard is applied to price increases that genuinely reflect higher supply costs, and the federal treasury would bear enforcement costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and fuel sellers facing fines

drawbacks.text: The core standard — prices that are 'unconscionably excessive' or take 'unfair advantage' — is vague, and even a good-faith seller whose costs genuinely spike during an emergency could face costly enforcement, though the text lists factors like actual added costs and market conditions for courts to weigh [S3].
The bill exempts transactions on futures markets, where much of the price run-up during oil market emergencies is set, so the largest price-formation venue is left out of the ban [S3].

Money for the Consumer Relief Trust Fund is only available 'to the extent provided for in advance in appropriations Acts,' so even fines that are collected would not automatically reach low-income households unless Congress appropriates the money [S3].
If the FTC files a federal action, state attorneys general are barred from suing the same defendant while that case is pending, which could slow state-level enforcement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the benefit is real but targeted: it only applies after the President declares an energy emergency, so it is no ordinary consumer protection. Weighing honestly, the main design flaws are the vague pricing standard (mitigated somewhat by the list of factors courts must consider), the carve-out for futures markets, and the fact that relief money still requires a congressional appropriation. On balance it would have given drivers and low-income families protection and funding at the expense of excess profits by large fuel sellers during crises — a trade a consumer would likely take.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and their subcommittees, never got a hearing or a vote, and quietly expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bart Stupak introduced the bill on April 27, 2009, with 32 original cosponsors, mostly Democrats [S1][S3][S5].

It grew to 41 cosponsors — 40 of 253 House Democrats and 1 of 178 House Republicans — but was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Education and Labor Committees, then split among three subcommittees on April 28 and June 4, 2009 [S4][S5].
The action history shows nothing after the June 4, 2009 subcommittee referral: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote. The bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies, refiners, and fuel sellers are better off because the bill died: they face no federal price-gouging penalty during emergencies, and no fines flow to a fund for low-income energy aid. Drivers and low-income households gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and fuel sellers; no gouging penalty

for.name: Rep. Bart Stupak
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban fuel price gouging during energy emergencies

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 27, 2009 and sent it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Environment and the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection; the record shows no hearing or markup ever followed

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to the Subcommittee on Healthy Families and Communities on June 4, 2009; no further action appears in the record

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 40 of 41 cosponsors were Democrats, with one Republican — but the bill died without ever facing a floor vote, so the House as a whole never took a position.

industries.note: Would have faced civil fines up to three times excess profits or $3 million during declared emergencies, plus DOJ criminal fines up to $150 million for corporations, with the FTC instructed to target companies over $500 million in annual fuel sales. Their pricing freedom during crises is exactly what the bill would have restricted, which is why the public benefit and the industry's cost pull in opposite directions.
The bill explicitly excludes futures-market transactions from the ban, so the market where large fuel price swings are set stays outside the price-gouging rules entirely.
Would have gained a new consumer-protection enforcement authority over fuel sellers, with a mandate to prioritize the largest companies.
Would have gained authority to sue in federal court on behalf of residents and collect civil penalties, on top of their existing state-law powers.
